claim: Nanobodies (nAbs) are the recombinant minimal antigen binding fragments derived from the atypical monomeric immunoglobulins present in camelid mammals and cartilaginous fish.
source: Nanobodies (nAbs) are the recombinant minimal antigen binding fragments derived from the atypical monomeric immunoglobulins present in camelid mammals and cartilaginous fish (Hamers-Casterman et al., 1993; Muyldermans, 2013; Desmyter et al., 2015; Beghein and Gettemans, 2017; Könning et al., 2017; De Meyer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature establishing the origin and nature of nanobodies.

claim: nAbs are ideally suited for use as intracellular antibodies (intrabodies) in living cells.
source: nAbs are ideally suited for use as intracellular antibodies (intrabodies) in living cells (Lafaye et al., 2009; Beghein et al., 2016; Staus et al., 2014; Bertier et al., 2017; Van Audenhove and Gettemans, 2016; Schumacher et al., 2018), as they fold efficiently and remain stable under a wide range of conditions, including the reducing cytoplasmic environment (Gahrtz and Conrad, 2009; Böldicke et al., 2005; Goenaga et al., 2007; Lynch et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies demonstrating the utility of nAbs as intrabodies.

claim: nAbs fold efficiently and remain stable under a wide range of conditions, including the reducing cytoplasmic environment.
source: nAbs are ideally suited for use as intracellular antibodies (intrabodies) in living cells (Lafaye et al., 2009; Beghein et al., 2016; Staus et al., 2014; Bertier et al., 2017; Van Audenhove and Gettemans, 2016; Schumacher et al., 2018), as they fold efficiently and remain stable under a wide range of conditions, including the reducing cytoplasmic environment (Gahrtz and Conrad, 2009; Böldicke et al., 2005; Goenaga et al., 2007; Lynch et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies on nAb stability.

claim: The small size of nAbs (≈1/10 of conventional IgG antibodies) improves penetration of cell or tissue samples.
source: In addition to their potential utility as intrabodies, nAbs also have advantages as immunolabeling reagents, as their small size (≈1/10 of conventional IgG antibodies) improves penetration of the cell or tissue samples (Perruchini et al., 2009; Fang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies demonstrating improved tissue penetration.

claim: nAbs improve imaging resolution by reducing the distance between the immunolabeling signal and the target protein from the 10–20 nm obtained with conventional primary and secondary antibodies down to 2–4 nm.
source: Importantly, nAbs improve imaging resolution by reducing the distance between the immunolabeling signal and the target protein from the 10–20 nm obtained with conventional primary and secondary antibodies down to 2–4 nm (Beghein and Gettemans, 2017; Ries et al., 2012; Szymborska et al., 2013; Pleiner et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies on imaging resolution improvements.

claim: Mammalian brain neurons express proteins estimated to encompass the products of two-thirds of the genome.
source: Integral to the functional complexity of neurons is the diversity of proteins they express (estimated to encompass the products of two-thirds of the genome), a complexity markedly enhanced by compartmentalization of specific proteins at highly restricted sites within the neuron's complex structure.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about neuronal protein diversity.

claim: Homer1 is a postsynaptic scaffolding protein present at partially overlapping sets of excitatory synapses.
source: These targets are the postsynaptic scaffolding proteins Homer1 (Brandstätter et al., 2004), IRSp53 (Soltau et al., 2002), and SAPAP2 (Takeuchi et al., 1997) that are present at partially overlapping sets of excitatory synapses
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on Homer1 localization.

claim: IRSp53 is a postsynaptic scaffolding protein present at partially overlapping sets of excitatory synapses.
source: These targets are the postsynaptic scaffolding proteins Homer1 (Brandstätter et al., 2004), IRSp53 (Soltau et al., 2002), and SAPAP2 (Takeuchi et al., 1997) that are present at partially overlapping sets of excitatory synapses
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on IRSp53 localization.

claim: SAPAP2 is a postsynaptic scaffolding protein present at partially overlapping sets of excitatory synapses.
source: These targets are the postsynaptic scaffolding proteins Homer1 (Brandstätter et al., 2004), IRSp53 (Soltau et al., 2002), and SAPAP2 (Takeuchi et al., 1997) that are present at partially overlapping sets of excitatory synapses
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on SAPAP2 localization.

claim: Gephyrin is found postsynaptically at most inhibitory synapses.
source: Gephyrin (Kneussel et al., 2001) found postsynaptically at most inhibitory synapses
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on Gephyrin localization.

claim: AMIGO-1 is a Kv2 channel auxiliary subunit found in large clusters at endoplasmic reticulum-plasma membrane (ER-PM) junctions present on the soma, proximal dendrites and AIS.
source: and the Kv2 channel auxiliary subunit AMIGO-1 (36) found in large clusters at endoplasmic reticulum-plasma membrane (ER-PM) junctions present on the soma, proximal dendrites and AIS.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation (reference 36) to prior literature on AMIGO-1 localization.

source: We subjected this phage display library (complexity ≈ 8 × 107) to panning against the individual purified recombinant target proteins immobilized in wells of a microtiter plate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the phage display library construction.

claim: The vast majority of COS-1 cells expressing EGFP- or EYFP-tagged nAb alone had substantial fluorescence signal in the nucleus.
source: We found that the vast majority of COS-1 cells expressing EGFP- or EYFP-tagged nAb alone had substantial fluorescence signal in the nucleus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Target protein coexpression led to a change in nAb subcellular localization, which was interpreted as being due to nAb binding to the cytoplasmic- or ER-localized target protein.
source: We next evaluated whether target protein coexpression led to a change in nAb subcellular localization, which we interpreted as being due to nAb binding to the cytoplasmic- or ER-localized target protein.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations and interpretation of the data.

claim: The expression and subcellular localization of the endogenous target proteins were not altered by nAb expression.
source: Importantly, the expression and subcellular localization of the endogenous target proteins were not altered by nAb expression, as quantified by a lack of significant change in target protein puncta size (Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Expression of the nAbs against target proteins at excitatory synapses did not impact the sizes of PSD-95 puncta.
source: Moreover, expression of the nAbs against target proteins at excitatory synapses did not impact the sizes of PSD-95 puncta (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The sizes of the puncta of Gephyrin and Synapsin immunolabeling were not impacted by expression of anti-Gephyrin nAbs.
source: The sizes of the puncta of Gephyrin and Synapsin immunolabeling were not impacted by expression of anti-Gephyrin nAbs (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 5.

claim: The sizes of AMIGO-1 and Kv2.1 puncta were not impacted by expression of anti-AMIGO-1 nAbs.
source: The sizes of AMIGO-1 and Kv2.1 puncta were not impacted by expression of anti-AMIGO-1 nAbs (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 5.

claim: Anti-Homer1 nAbs such as HC20 and HC87 exhibited precise colocalization with Homer1 immunolabeling after long-term expression.
source: An analysis of the localization of a number of anti-Homer1 nAb-YFP fusions after such long-term expression revealed that a subset of the nAb-YFP fusions (green), such as HC20 and HC87, exhibited precise colocalization with Homer1 immunolabeling (red), with little or no detectable signal in dendritic shafts, consistent with their binding to and accumulation at Homer1 clustered in dendritic spines (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Long-term expression of anti-Homer1 nAbs did not lead to significant changes in the overall sizes or density of Homer1 puncta.
source: In spite of these differences in binding, in no case did long-term expression of the anti-Homer1 nAbs lead to significant changes in the overall sizes or density of Homer1 puncta (Figure 2D), showing that the long-term expression of these nAbs and their binding to synaptic Homer1 did not detectably impact Homer1 expression and localization.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The nAb-GFP puncta were marking stable structures present in the TIRF field over the course of one-minute recordings collected at 1 Hz.
source: Over the course of one-minute recordings collected at 1 Hz, we observed that the nAb-GFP puncta (which we observed colocalized with the target proteins in the experiments mentioned in the previous section) were marking stable structures present in the TIRF field, such that overlaid time-lapse images of nAb-GFP localization yielded tightly colocalized structures (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claim: A substantial subset (33/39) of the ELISA-positive anti-Homer1 nAb BC supes tested exhibited robust immunolabeling of fixed and permeabilized COS-1 cells expressing Homer1L.
source: We found that a substantial subset (33/39) of the ELISA-positive anti-Homer1 nAb BC supes tested exhibited robust immunolabeling of fixed and permeabilized COS-1 cells expressing Homer1L.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunolabeling assays.

claim: None of the unique ELISA-positive nAb BC supes against the other targets (IRSp53, SAPAP2, Gephyrin, AMIGO-1) yielded detectable immunoreactivity in the COS-1 cell IF-ICC assay.
source: In contrast, none of the unique ELISA-positive nAb BC supes against the other targets yielded detectable immunoreactivity in this assay (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: A large proportion (25/33) of the anti-Homer1 BC supes tested yielded robust immunolabeling of brain sections.
source: We found that a large proportion (25/33) of the BC supes tested yielded robust immunolabeling of brain sections, with the remainder exhibiting no detectable immunolabeling (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: Each of the 25 brain IHC-positive nAbs was also scored as positive in the heterologous COS-1 cell IF-ICC assay.
source: Each of the 25 brain IHC-positive nAbs was also scored as positive in the heterologous COS-1 cell IF-ICC assay.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from both IHC and IF-ICC assays.

claim: The pattern of immunolabeling obtained with the anti-Homer1 nAbs matched closely that obtained with validated anti-Homer1 mouse mAbs.
source: The pattern of immunolabeling obtained with the anti-Homer1 nAbs matched closely that obtained with validated anti-Homer1 mouse mAbs (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative immunolabeling data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Directly conjugated Alexa647 nAb had the smallest overall cluster size compared to unlabeled nAb detected with Alexa647-conjugated anti-HA antibody and conventional mAb detected with Alexa647-conjugated secondary antibody.
source: As shown in Figure 5, there was a significant difference in the size of immunolabeled puncta for each of the labeling reagent combinations used. Directly conjugated Alexa647 nAb had the smallest overall cluster size, followed by the unlabeled nAb detected with the Alexa647-conjugated anti-HA antibody, with the conventional mAb detected with an Alexa647-conjugated secondary antibody having the largest cluster size (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative super-resolution imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: A subset of the unique ELISA-positive nAbs against Homer1 (13/39) detected a single robust band at the characteristic electrophoretic mobility of Homer1 (≈47 kDa).
source: We found that a subset of the unique ELISA-positive nAbs against Homer1 (13/39; Table 1) detected a single robust band at the characteristic electrophoretic mobility of Homer1 (≈47 kDa) (Saito et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data and citation to prior literature on Homer1 molecular weight.

claim: A small subset of the unique ELISA-positive nAbs against Gephyrin (2/24) detected a single band at the characteristic electrophoretic mobility (≈80 kDa) of Gephyrin.
source: A small subset of the unique ELISA-positive nAbs against Gephyrin (2/24; Table 1) detected a single band at the characteristic electrophoretic mobility (≈80 kDa) of Gephyrin (Feng et al., 1998) that comigrated with the immunoreactive band for the validated anti-Gephyrin mouse mAb L106/93 (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6 and citation to prior literature on Gephyrin molecular weight.

claim: No specific immunolabeling was detected with any of the ELISA-positive nAb BC supes against IRSp53, SAPAP2, or AMIGO-1 in immunoblot applications.
source: No specific immunolabeling was detected with any of the ELISA-positive nAb BC supes against the other targets (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: The nAbs developed in this study have little discernible impact on the expression and subcellular localization of their endogenous targets when expressed in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: These results indicate that these nAbs act as intrabodies that recognize their endogenous target proteins in CHNs, and the expression of the nAbs has little discernible impact on the expression and subcellular localization of their endogenous targets.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations and quantitative analyses of target protein expression and localization.

claim: Immunizations to increase the representation of high affinity binders in the llama were used as the source of the nAb cDNA library.
source: However, these approaches often yield low affinity binders that need to be matured by molecular evolution in vitro (Gustchina et al., 2009; Gram et al., 1992; Jackson et al., 1995), which is a time and labor-consuming process. Therefore, we elected to use immunizations to increase the representation of high affinity binders in the llama used as the source of our nAb cDNA library.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on affinity maturation and the authors' methodological choice.

claim: The overall strategy generated at least one nAb that functioned as an intrabody in neurons for each of the five targeted brain proteins.
source: Our overall strategy generated at least one nAb that functioned as an intrabody in neurons for each of the five targeted brain proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results summarized in Table 1.

claim: The nAbs that were evaluated by live cell imaging label stable structures within cultured rat hippocampal neurons.
source: That the nAbs we evaluated by live cell imaging label stable structures within cultured rat hippocampal neurons suggests that the nAbs are primarily binding their targets at final subcellular location, as opposed to binding to the proteins while in transit to these sites, or otherwise targeting mobile structures.
evidence: This claim is based on live cell imaging data shown in Figure 3 and the authors' interpretation.

claim: A subset of anti-Homer1 nAbs exhibit enhanced resolution in super-resolution light microscopy.
source: These nAbs exhibit the enhanced resolution in super-resolution light microscopy predicted for such nanoscale labeling reagents (Beghein and Gettemans, 2017; Ries et al., 2012; Szymborska et al., 2013; Pleiner et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by super-resolution imaging data shown in Figure 5 and citations to prior literature predicting this enhancement.

claim: Among the five proteins targeted in the nAb development efforts, only the Homer1 nAb project yielded large pools of nAbs positive for immunolabeling transfected heterologous cells and brain sections.
source: It is surprising to us that among the five proteins targeted in the nAb development efforts described here, only the Homer1 nAb project yielded large pools of nAbs positive for immunolabeling transfected heterologous cells and brain sections (Table 1), given that we had previously performed mouse mAb projects against each of these targets, using the same recombinant proteins as immunogens and in screening, and for each obtained a substantial number of mAbs positive for these applications (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Table 1 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: A retrospective analysis of the antiserum from the immunized llama by IF-ICC against transfected COS-1 cells expressing the individual target proteins yielded substantial immunolabeling only for cells expressing Homer1.
source: However, a retrospective analysis of the antiserum from the immunized llama by IF-ICC against transfected COS-1 cells expressing the individual target proteins yielded substantial immunolabeling only for cells expressing Homer1 (not shown), suggesting a fundamental lack of an immune response against epitopes preserved in aldehyde-fixed samples, and not a failure of phage display selection to capture immunolabeling-competent nAbs.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations from retrospective analysis.

claim: The positive anti-Homer1 nAbs exhibited substantial immunolabeling of neuropil in caudate putamen (CPU), cerebral cortex (CTX) and hippocampus (HC).
source: As shown in Figure 4A for nAb HS15, the positive anti-Homer1 nAbs exhibited substantial immunolabeling of neuropil in caudate putamen (CPU), cerebral cortex (CTX) and hippocampus (HC).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Immunolabeling for the positive anti-Homer1 nAbs was especially prominent in subiculum and CA1 stratum oriens and radiatum in hippocampus.
source: In hippocampus, immunolabeling for the positive anti-Homer1 nAbs (note that the HS12 nAb was scored as negative in this application) was especially prominent in subiculum and CA1 stratum oriens and radiatum (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: All nAbs that showed positive immunolabeling in brain regions also had strong signals in olfactory bulb, and relatively weak or undetectable labeling in numerous other brain regions (thalamus, globus pallidus, brainstem, cerebellum).
source: All nAbs that showed positive immunolabeling in these areas also had strong signals in olfactory bulb, and relatively weak or undetectable labeling in numerous other brain regions (thalamus, globus pallidus, brainstem, cerebellum), consistent with Homer1 mRNA expression in brain (Clifton et al., 2017; Lein et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and citations to prior literature on Homer1 mRNA expression.

claim: The nAb labeling pattern matched the localization of Homer1 protein from previous IHC studies.
source: Furthermore, the nAb labeling pattern matched the localization of Homer1 protein from previous IHC studies (Shiraishi et al., 2004; Shiraishi-Yamaguchi and Furuichi, 2007), and immunolabeling obtained with anti-Homer1 mAbs recognizing both the long and short (L113/130) or only the long (L113/27) splice variants (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with prior literature and imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Immunolabeling with a directly labeled nAb allows for enhanced resolution of target detection in super-resolution light microscopy.
source: This provides an empirical demonstration that immunolabeling with a directly labeled nAb allows for enhanced resolution of target detection in super-resolution light microscopy.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The band recognized by the anti-Homer1 nAbs had characteristics corresponding to the band obtained with the validated anti-Homer1 mouse mAb L113/130.
source: The band recognized by the nAbs had characteristics corresponding to the band obtained with the validated anti-Homer1 mouse mAb L113/130 (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The immunoreactive band for anti-Gephyrin nAbs comigrated with the immunoreactive band for the validated anti-Gephyrin mouse mAb L106/93.
source: A small subset of the unique ELISA-positive nAbs against Gephyrin (2/24; Table 1) detected a single band at the characteristic electrophoretic mobility (≈80 kDa) of Gephyrin (Feng et al., 1998) that comigrated with the immunoreactive band for the validated anti-Gephyrin mouse mAb L106/93 (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The nAbs developed in this study represent a valuable toolbox of reagents available to the neuroscience community for diverse applications.
source: In summary, we have generated a series of validated nAbs against neuronal proteins selectively expressed in specific subcellular compartments in brain neurons. These nAbs represent a valuable toolbox of reagents available to the neuroscience community for diverse applications.
evidence: This claim is based on the overall results of the study and represents the authors' conclusion.

claim: The pipeline employed in this study can be used in developing nAbs against other neuronal targets to enhance the spectrum of experimental approaches available to researchers.
source: The pipeline we employed is an exemplar that can be used in developing nAbs against other neuronal targets to enhance the spectrum of experimental approaches available to researchers.
evidence: This claim represents the authors' conclusion about the broader applicability of their methodology.
